claims.text: Spark plasma sintering can enable a large-scale in situ reaction between RHEA powders and copper.
Spark plasma sintering can produce a stable RHEA–Cu composite microstructure despite positive refractory-element/Cu mixing enthalpy.
The initial material is a mixed powder blend containing refractory HEA components and Cu.
Rapid heating and a short SPS dwell time can initiate and control the RHEA–Cu reaction.
High-temperature SPS under an inert atmosphere with rapid heating and controlled dwell time limits excessive diffusion and prevents undesirable phase formation.
Electrical Joule heating during SPS promotes a transient high-temperature reaction zone at particle interfaces.
The transient interfacial reaction zone forms a dense, in situ bonded interface between the RHEA and Cu.
Localized rapid thermal activation during SPS overcomes the thermodynamic barrier associated with positive RHEA–Cu mixing enthalpy.
Rapid SPS locks in a fine, stable microstructure before significant phase segregation occurs.
SPS will produce a homogeneous RHEA–Cu composite with well-dispersed phases and strong interfacial bonding.
The resulting composite should have improved mechanical integrity and high-temperature stability.
Conventional melting or slow sintering often produces coarse microstructures and significant phase agglomeration because of unfavorable RHEA–Cu mixing enthalpy.
Excessively long SPS dwell times or overly high temperatures may cause undesirable intermetallic phases or grain coarsening.
Successful RHEA–Cu processing depends on careful optimization of SPS parameters.
The reaction kinetics, interfacial phases, and reproducibility at larger scales require experimental validation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis asserts that SPS can enable a large-scale RHEA–Cu reaction, while the uncertainty field states that reproducibility at larger scales remains to be experimentally established.
